items.title: Don't Go Monolithic; the Agent Stack Is Stratifying
items.story_key: story|title:don t go monolithic the agent stack is stratifying
items.content_excerpt: The defensible asset in enterprise AI is not the model. It’s the organizational world model. Every major compute era decomposes into specialized layers with different winners at each level. Cloud split into IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS. The modern data stack split into ingestion, warehousing, transformation, and BI. Each time, specialists beat the generalists because each layer has its own economics: its own rate of change, capital requirements, and sources of lock-in. The enterprise AI agent stack is doing the same thing right now. Arvind Jain, the CEO of Glean, recently published a structural analysis of the emerging enterprise agent architecture that crystallized something I’d been thinking about. He describes a stack splitting into six layers (security, context, models, orchestration, agents, and interfaces), and each layer is defensible to a different degree. Glean sits in the context layer so the usual positioning caveats apply, but the structural argument is sound regardless of who makes it. The three sections below cover models converging toward shared infrastructure, the two depths of the context layer, and the compounding flywheel that context and orchestration form. The model layer is converging fastest toward commodity economics. Training costs scale roughly 2.4x per year , with current frontier runs costing hundreds of millions and billion-dollar training runs already underway , according to Anthropic’s Dario Amodei. Only a handful of organizations on Earth can operate at this scale: OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Anthropic, Meta, and a few others including xAI and Mistral. This is capital-intensive infrastructure, with the same structure as semiconductor fabs or cloud hyperscalers. I expect foundation models to become shared utilities, so no enterprise will build a moat on one. Companies already act on this. 37% of enterprises now use five or more models in production , up from 29% the prior year. Different tasks demand different models: Claude for code and tool use, GPT for extended reasoning, Gemini Flash for low-latency routing, specialized models for image generation and embeddings. Betting your enterprise stack on a single model provider carries the same risk as betting it on a single cloud. Open standards like Anthropic’s Model Context Protocol , now hosted by the Linux Foundation with 97 million monthly SDK downloads, and Google’s Agent-to-Agent protocol are making this multi-model enterprise AI architecture practical. items.title: Show HN: Neon and Mubit: an agent that cuts its own frontier-model tokens by 73%
items.story_key: story|title:neon and mubit an agent that cuts its own frontier model tokens by 73
items.content_excerpt: An agent on Neon Functions, Lakebase Postgres, and AI Gateway that hands its routine steps to a small model tuned on its own traffic Mubit is middleware for AI agents. It sits between your agent and the model with a one-line endpoint change, learns from every call, and moves recurring steps to small models tuned on your own traffic, while the frontier model keeps the hard ones. There's nothing extra to host. To show how that works with Neon, they built a template for cutting frontier-model token spend - an agent on Neon Functions and Lakebase Postgres that sends every model call through Mubit to Neon AI Gateway . The example workload is a data analyst agent that answers business questions over Postgres, but the setup applies to any agent on Neon that calls frontier models through AI Gateway: Once Mubit has tuned a small model for the routine steps, it serves them itself, and lessons from verified runs help the agent avoid repeating mistakes. In the example workload, using Mubit cut the agent's gpt-5.5 tokens by 73% and made it 40% faster, without losing accuracy. "Neon gives agents a database and a model endpoint in one place. Mubit sits in between and learns from every call, so an agent on Neon gets cheaper and more reliable the more it runs" — Anil Peri, CEO at Mubit "We built AI Gateway so agents on Neon can call frontier models through one endpoint. Mubit is a good example of what you can put in front of it. The agent passes the repetitive stuff to small models, and when your schema changes, it drops what's out of date and figures out the new tables on its own" — Bryan Clark, Product Lead at Databricks Teams often build an agent on a frontier model and send every call to it. That's quite inefficient token-wise - cost and latency grow with every step, and a lot of those steps are routine - you end up paying frontier prices for work that doesn't need a frontier model. Mubit measured this with the template's example agent. On their benchmark, gpt-5.5 alone needed about 10 model calls, 21.7k gpt-5.5 input tokens, and 26 seconds to answer one question. Most of those calls were mechanical, like listing tables, reading table definitions, and writing up an answer the query had already found. Only the SQL steps actually needed the frontier model. Agents also don't remember what they've learned. items.content_excerpt: Today, we're open-sourcing Edge0-145B and Edge0-120B , together with our unified inference framework and deployment tools. Edge0-145B is the world's first open-source on-device AI model with 145 billion parameters. It brings coding, reasoning, and agent capabilities that rival frontier cloud models to your own computer. On-device AI has long forced a tradeoff between model capability and what the hardware can run. Larger models demand more memory, bandwidth, and power; smaller models can struggle with complex work. Moving that work to the cloud adds model-provider fees, data-handling constraints, and a dependence on connectivity. We're releasing the full stack so developers can reproduce the results, evaluate or fine-tune the models, and integrate them into their own products. Get the model weights , explore the inference framework , or try the Edge0 App . Edge0-145B makes a 145-billion-parameter model usable on a personal laptop. items.summary:
Release: llm-gemini 0.37

Google launched Gemini 4 Hydrogen today - the lowest cost member of the Gemini 4 family.

It's actually not too far off the price of its much bigger siblings, Carbon and Argon. I'm finding Gemini 4's pricing really confusing. Here's the pricing scheme:

Model Dates Input ($/M) Cached input Output
Gemini 4 Carbon Through Nov 30, 2026 $2.00 $0.10 $10.00
From Dec 1, 2026 $4.00 $0.20 $20.00
Gemini 4 Argon Through Nov 30, 2026 $2.00 $0.10 $10.00
From Dec 1, 2026 $4.00 $0.20 $20.00
Gemini 4 Hydrogen   $1.50 $0.075 $7.50

Carbon and Argon are the same price, and both are scheduled to double in price on December 1st. If they're the same price, why have two different models? Google says that Argon "delivers Gemini 4 intelligence with faster responses and lower token spend per turn compared to Gemini 4 Carbon" - so it may be priced the same, but it will use less tokens per task.

Hydrogen, supposedly the cheap model, is currently only a 25% discount on its more capable peers. The Hydrogen price will make more sense after December 1st, when it will represent a 75% discount. It's still considerably more expensive than Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna - they're both $0.10/$0.50, so Hydrogen is 15x that.

I had Hydrogen generate some pelicans. Here's a full comparison grid showing the pelicans for all three members of the Gemini 4 family at their three supported effort levels:

Considering how close they are in price, the difference in pelican quality for Hydrogen is quite stark.

Here's how Google describe Hydrogen's intended position in their mix of models:

In real-world software development, while teams rely on frontier models like Carbon and Argon for deep architectural judgment when designing systems or untangling subtle bugs, they still need a fast, disciplined execution model for writing code, running tests, and verifying changes. Hydrogen is built to stand on its own as a model for everyday work — or to pair with Carbon and Argon as the high-efficiency execution engine in multi-model workflows.

Most notably, Hydrogen is the new free tier model, and is the model that will power AI features in Google Search.

items.title: Inkling 2 Small on vLLM: Day-0 Support
items.summary: vLLM supports Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small from day 0: attention residuals, a new decode kernel for relative-bias attention, all-reduce fused with the ops around it, and DSpark speculative decoding.
items.story_key: model:vllm|variant:small|title:inkling 2 small on vllm day 0 support
items.content_excerpt: vLLM supports Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small on day 0. It is a multimodal (text and vision) MoE model with 594B total and 17B active parameters and up to 1M tokens of context. The model also comes with a native DSpark speculator. vLLM supports it with optimized performance (up to 630 TPS/user at TP4 and acceptance length 3.5) and also supports LoRA. Figure 1. Inkling 2 Small architecture. Gold marks what is new or changed since Inkling. Inkling backbone + recent advances. Inkling 2 Small keeps Inkling's backbone: the 5:1 mix of sliding-window and full attention, GQA with a learned relative bias instead of RoPE, the four short convolutions per layer and a sigmoid-routed MoE. On top of it, it adds recent advances. Block attention residuals replace the residual stream, so before each sublayer a learned query mixes the outputs of earlier 6-layer blocks. Gated attention puts a sigmoid gate on each head's output, together with a per-token attention sink . It replaces the hMLP image encoder with a 23-layer ViT. Mixed-precision MoE with Four-Over-Six NVFP4. Out of Inkling 2 Small's 48 layers, the experts of the first 40 use NVFP4 and those of the last 8 use MXFP8. The NVFP4 activations use a per-token global scale plus dual-candidate block scales ( Four Over Six ): for each 16-element block, the quantizer tries scaling the block's maximum to 6 and to 4, and keeps whichever gives the lower reconstruction error (MAE). DSpark speculator with an RNN head. The checkpoint also ships a DSpark draft in place of Inkling's 8 chained MTP heads. The speculator has 5 layers and drafts 7 tokens per step. The head is the RNN variant that DeepSeek's DSpark paper described. Kernel fusion and PDL. vLLM aggressively fuses the collective communication and memory-bound ops between sublayers into a single kernel. With attention residuals, each boundary needs an all-reduce, a short convolution, a residual update, the attention-residual mix and an RMSNorm: five memory-bound steps on the same hidden states. The fused kernel, allreduce_conv_mix (gold in Figure 2), runs the all-reduce over NVLink multicast and keeps everything after it in registers. The GEMM, attention, routing and activation kernels launch with programmatic dependent launch (PDL), so each one's prologue overlaps the tail of the previous kernel, which matters at small batch sizes, where a decode step is a long chain of short kernels. items.title: LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B
items.story_key: story|ver:4.1|title:llmon an llm native markup language now in granite 4 1 3b and 8b
items.content_excerpt: LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens. Over a long trajectory, the context fills with numerous types of components: a system prompt, past conversation turns, instructions that act on retrieved documents, tool responses or user data, requirements constraining the allowed output, and reasoning chains. The context carries a rich structure, most of which is either implicit to the model or encoded in formats such as JSON that were not designed to be digested by LLMs. This is one of the main reasons LLMs, particularly those on the smaller end of the scale, are brittle and sometimes fail in unexpected ways. The lack of explicit structure can also be exploited by attackers, for example, in the form of prompt injections. To address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models. Semantically coherent components are marked with meaningful tags which are wrapped in reserved special-token delimiters. Data schemas, including nesting, are stated in a way that is unambiguous to a causal LLM. Unique IDs make it possible to point to specific instructions, which could reside anywhere in the context, and bind them to the data payloads they should act on, analogous to the way functions are called and arguments are passed to them in programming languages. Today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview . We are also releasing a GitHub repo, which includes a toolkit for working with LLMON and examples of workflows and templates. JSON was designed for parsers, not for causal language models. The tokenizer is not constrained to respect the grammar, and structure is encoded by tokens ({, ", :) that may also appear in normal text. To a model, a quotation mark inside a document and a quotation mark that closes a field are the same token. Escaping rules that are clear to a parser are only statistical patterns to a model. Nesting depth is encoded by counting brackets, which transformers are known to be weak at, especially over long spans. LLMON, on the other hand, is an XML-like markup whose structural delimiters are reserved special tokens rather than characters, so structure and content use separate parts of the vocabulary.   • Added to claude plugin validate the $ nouns a mod's engine.create hook adds, withholds or replaces

  • Added an options menu (stop, switch to usage credits, upgrade) when a model needs usage credits that are turned off or used up
  • Added a progress heartbeat every 30 seconds while hooks run long in claude -p and SDK sessions, so a host such as Claude Desktop won't end the turn as hung (once it includes this version)
  • Added .docx support to Artifact tool asset uploads
  • Added a /diff to close hint to the diff panel, and the keys that focus and close a panel to the ? shortcut guide

items.content_excerpt: Frontier cloud LLMs carry high operational costs that can fluctuate unexpectedly, and relying on such third-party models introduces vulnerabilities, as providers can modify, deny, or deprecate access at any time. Furthermore, proprietary models offer limited customization for specific workflows, while posing risks to privacy, data control, and transparency. Besides, not every task demands frontier-level intelligence: small, specialized agents can be equally capable on specific tasks and significantly cheaper to run, since many routine or smaller workloads can be processed efficiently on-device. As intelligence per parameter continues to improve rapidly, we aim to stand at the forefront of this shift toward performant, privacy-focused, self-hosted models. Tether AI Research introduces BotPsy , a 0.8B-parameter model introduce BotPsy , a 0.8B-parameter model designed for function calling and agentic workflows, built on top of Qwen3.5-0.8B and suitable for on-device deployment. BotPsy is a "personal assistant" that uses tools to perform a variety of simple tasks for the user, in domains such as web search & research, travel & lifestyle, commerce & finance, business & customer operations, device & vehicle control, files & documents, calendar, and email & messaging. Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty. BotPsy achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) tool-use and agentic performance for its size, outperforming every model of up to 1.2B parameters that we tested (Figures 1 and 2). Designed for secure on-device workflows, it provides exceptional instruction-following reliability and efficiency while keeping user data private. items.title: LM-SimBench: A Unified Framework, Dataset, and Benchmark for Large Language Model Training Simulation
items.summary: Evaluating candidate parallelization strategies through distributed training runs makes strategy selection prohibitively expensive at scale. Performance simulation offers a lower cost alternative, yet controlled comparisons among existing simulators remain difficult because they differ in the training stages they model and the workloads on which they are evaluated. We introduce LM-SimBench, a unified framework, profiling dataset, and benchmark for evaluating LLM training simulators. The framework decomposes simulation into functional stages from model compilation to schedule level aggregation, connecting execution representations and cost estimators to measurable evaluation targets. Following this framework, we profile 23 model settings from 10 dense and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLM families on an Ascend Neural Processing Unit (NPU) cluster. The resulting dataset contains 348 feasible configurations that jointly vary five parallelism dimensions and activation recomputation, with six views spanning configuration, rank, operator, event, and kernel granularity. Evaluations of representative training simulators demonstrate how LM-SimBench supports comparisons of prediction accuracy, assessment of configuration selection, and diagnosis of prediction errors. Matched GPU-NPU experiments validate the cross-platform applicability of the collection and evaluation protocol and demonstrate NPU-guided GPU configuration selection.

items.title: One Policy for 100 Household Tasks: Our Solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge
items.summary: We describe our solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge: 100 long-horizon household tasks in the OmniGibson simulator. We placed 9th on the final leaderboard, the only independent team in the top 10. The core of the solution is a single vision-language-action (VLA) model, one checkpoint for all 100 tasks, built on our 1st-place 2025 solution, which is based on $π_{0.5}$. On the 50 tasks shared with 2025, its Q rises from 0.260 to 0.371; across all 100 tasks it scores 0.392. Our main conclusion from 2025 was that the model was undertrained, so most of the 2026 work went into training the model for longer, optimizing some training parameters, making each training step slightly faster and reducing the gradient noise: a migration from 50 to 100 tasks (semantic stages built from the demonstrations' skill annotations, task and stage embeddings of new tasks warm-started from similar old ones, and a 21-dimensional action space matching the teleoperation controls); variance-reduced multi-sample flow matching with a simple noise-vs-compute model that picks the number of action-expert samples per observation without ablations; and a 200k-step training run, about one pass over the 211M frames of the demonstrations. A cloud evaluation infrastructure keeps a shared record with provenance, episode diagnostics and restorable simulator states, and runs six simulators on one GPU together faster than real time. On top of the learned policy, 14 tasks are routed to a GPT-6 Astra coding agent that controls the robot through observation and motion tools, starting every episode from a frozen copy of its own practice session on training instances. Across these 14 tasks, Astra's mean Q is 0.639, against 0.108 for the learned policy. The public submission included only part of the Astra results and scored 0.446 Q with 27.3% full-task success.

items.title: Evaluating LLM-Generated World Models for Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning
items.summary: Formal world models can support planning, verification, and safety reasoning, but constructing them from open-ended natural-language situations is difficult, particularly in multi-agent settings where several formalizations may be plausible. We study whether five LLMs can generate such world models as partially observable stochastic games and whether mechanical validity is sufficient to establish that the resulting model faithfully represents the intended decision problem. We introduce a benchmark of 44 scenarios spanning game, situational, and cultural settings and evaluate generated world models along three dimensions: mechanical validity, reference-relative structural agreement, and semantic criteria. Across three empirical tracks, we analyze 410 first-pass generations. In the reference-backed game track, 134/135 generated world models pass a strict mechanical audit, yet mean permutation-invariant structural F1 is only 0.366, with just 28/134 mechanically valid models exactly matching the authored reference. In the cultural track, explicitly naming the country changes the generated structural representation for most LLMs while producing only small changes in automated semantic scores. These results show that executability is a necessary but insufficient criterion for LLM-generated world models: models that are mechanically valid can still differ substantially in the structure used by downstream neuro-symbolic reasoning and planning.

items.title: Article: LLM Reliability Layers Under Test: Accuracy, Yield, and the Limits of Verification
items.summary:
Verification layers sort outputs by trust rather than fixing errors. In a benchmark of six reliability layers, voting and self-correction failed to recover accuracy - they only withheld doubtful records. Production systems gain more reliability by replacing generation with deterministic lookups, tracking yield over raw accuracy, and resolving extraction bottlenecks before stacking checks.

By Pushpdeep Mishra, Wejdan Bagais

items.story_key: story|title:introducing alphaproof code a breakthrough in verifying complex software at dept
items.content_excerpt: How Google DeepMind researchers built a new agentic framework that formally verified the code of Signal’s cryptographic protocol — long considered to be a grand security challenge Today, we’re sharing a milestone in software security long considered to be a grand challenge: Google DeepMind researchers guided AI agents to mathematically prove key security properties of the actual code underlying the Signal protocol, the technology that protects billions of private conversations in apps like Signal and Google Messages. This breakthrough discovery was made using AlphaProof Code , a novel agentic framework for formal verification at unprecedented depth that combines human expertise with AI agents. Formal verification—mathematically proving code runs correctly without flaws—is the highest standard of security assurance; however, it is difficult and often labor-intensive. Our work marks the first time AI has been used to formally verify a widely deployed cryptographic protocol at this depth. It's also the first time the implementation of a widely deployed protocol like this has been formally verified by any method, with or without AI. AlphaProof Code is a multi-LLM agentic framework that splits the work of formal verification the way a research team would: human experts work with AI to decide what to prove, and a group of AI agents does it. First, our researchers collaborated with a mix of models to translate Signal’s security goals into formal mathematical specifications, with human experts reviewing every one. From there, agents powered by Gemini Carbon did the proofs, generating over six million lines of Lean, a computer language that mathematically proves the accuracy of code. Next, the agents audited the proof and highlighted areas that needed a second look by a human – just one percent of the codebase, a massive time savings. Because Lean automatically checks the rest, our experts could focus their review where human judgment matters most. Cryptographic protocols underpin nearly all digital communication, from online banking to web browsing, and a single flaw can expose millions of people at once. That's why experts have spent decades formally analyzing them. But most protocol verification stops at the design level.
